case_title: Dauvaram Nirmalkar v. State of Chhattisgarh
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (conviction altered to s.304 Part I, applying Exception 1 to s.300); Evidence Act s.106, ss.25-27 considered
evidence_type: Circumstantial (chain of facts); medical (post-mortem); recovery (pick-axe and blood-stained shirt); witness testimony (mostly hostile public witnesses, plus presence of PW-9 and PW-10)
confession: Appellant went to police station on 26 September 2011 and confessed. Held inadmissible under s.25 Evidence Act and not relied on as a confession; only the portion leading to discovery of the pick-axe was admissible under s.27.
mitigating_circumstances: Victim's alcohol addiction, abusive and ill-tempered conduct, and threats on the night of the incident; sudden loss of self-control; appellant had attempted suicide by holding live electrical wires
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC; life imprisonment, fine of Rs.1,000 with six months simple imprisonment in default
high_court_outcome: Criminal Appeal No. 400 of 2013 decided on 25.02.2019; the Supreme Court agreed with the High Court and trial court on the appellant's involvement. The judgment does not separately set out the High Court's exact disposition.
offence_finally_established: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder (IPC s.304 Part I)
neutral_facts: The victim and the accused were brothers living in the same house, although they occupied separate rooms. Relatives and neighbours described the victim as addicted to alcohol, frequently quarrelling with the accused, and abusive and ill-tempered. On the night of the incident the victim and the accused were together in the house. Witnesses present in the house that night, including two young relatives, did not describe any intruder or third person being present, and no such suggestion was put to them. The victim was later found in the house with multiple fractures of the skull on the left temporal, frontal, parietal and occipital regions, a deep lesion, and a lacerated wound on the chin. The post-mortem examination recorded that death was due to coma caused by shock from these head injuries. Following a disclosure made by the accused, a pick-axe was recovered from a wooden box in the house. The pick-axe and a shirt worn by the accused during the incident were found to be stained with blood. The accused had burn injuries to the hands and had earlier tried to end his life by holding live electrical wires. Most of the public witnesses examined were declared hostile, but they broadly deposed that the two men lived in separate rooms in the same house. The accused's defence was that a third person had killed the victim. The evidence showed that on the night of the incident the victim had consumed alcohol and told the accused to leave the house, failing which he would kill the accused.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from coma due to shock after multiple skull fractures; deep scalp lesion and lacerated wound on the chin
number_of_offences: 1 charged; 1 finally upheld (conviction altered to s.304 Part I)
premeditation_planning: Court did not find premeditation or planning; it held the killing followed sudden and grave provocation and a loss of self-control, bringing the case within Exception 1 to s.300.
motive: Alleged: the victim's alcohol addiction and abuse, which the prosecution relied on to show motive. The court treated the victim's abusive conduct and night-time threat as provocation.
key_evidence_accepted: Post-mortem evidence (PW-12); presence of appellant and victim together that night (PW-9, PW-10 evidence on presence); absence of any suggested intruder; recovery of blood-stained pick-axe and shirt on disclosure; appellant's admitted burn injuries; common evidence of victim's alcohol addiction and abuse (PW-3, PW-4, PW-8, PW-9, PW-10)
witness_credibility: Public witnesses declared hostile but, as the court found, deposed more or less in unison that the appellant and victim lived in separate rooms. PW-9's claim that PW-10 told her the appellant killed the victim was not supported by PW-10, who did not admit making it. The court accepted the common account of the victim's alcohol addiction and abusive behaviour.
post_offence_conduct: Appellant went to the police station on 26 September 2011 and confessed; his disclosure led to recovery of the pick-axe and the body. Court treated the disclosure-linked discovery as admissible under s.27.
custody_duration: In custody since 27 September 2011; over 10 years at the time of the Supreme Court judgment
trial_duration: offence: not given; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 25.02.2019; Supreme Court: 02.08.2022
legal_representation: Harinder Mohan Singh (for appellant); Sumeer Sodhi and Dhruv Wadhwa (for respondent State)
investigation_status: Post-mortem completed and proved; pick-axe seized on the appellant's disclosure; trial completed. Charge sheet filing not stated.
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 IPC, life imprisonment, fine Rs.1,000. High Court (Criminal Appeal No. 400 of 2013, 25.02.2019): conviction on involvement upheld as the Supreme Court agreed with it. Supreme Court: appeal partly allowed; conviction converted to s.304 Part I IPC and sentence reduced to time already undergone.
prosecution_argument: Not stated in the judgment as oral argument; the judgment records only that the prosecution relied on the victim's alcohol addiction and abuse to show motive and on the circumstantial chain of facts.
defence_argument: Not stated for Supreme Court oral submissions; at trial the appellant claimed a third person killed the victim, which the courts rejected.
legal_principle_applied: Exception 1 to s.300 IPC (grave and sudden provocation causing loss of self-control), applying the reasonable man test, the cumulative provocation principle with a verifiable final provocative act, and the Nanavati conditions; Evidence Act s.106 for facts within the appellant's knowledge; ss.25 and 27 on confessions and discovery.
precedent_relied_upon: K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra, [1962] 1 Suppl. SCR 567; Budhi Singh v. State of Himachal Pradesh, (2012) 13 SCC 663; Aghnoo Nagesia v. State of Bihar, [1966] 1 SCR 134; Rampal Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2012) 8 SCC 289 (referred to); R. v. Duffy, (1949) 1 All ER 932 (referred to)
sentencing_rationale: Appellant had already suffered over 10 years of incarceration; the sentence was modified to the period already undergone, with the conviction converted to s.304 Part I.
judicial_mitigating_factors: Victim's continuous alcohol-fuelled abuse and threats, followed by a final provocation on the night of the incident, causing sudden and grave provocation and loss of self-control; long period already in custody
other_sentence_order: Appellant to be released forthwith on payment of fine or default imprisonment, if not required in any other case
